tools.desc: The best-known AI chatbot. It answers questions, helps you write, makes pictures, searches the web and can talk out loud.
tools.name: ChatGPT
tools.start: Sign up for free. Then ask it to explain something you have always wondered about.

tools.desc: An AI chatbot known for careful, natural writing and for reading long documents. It is also strong at coding and at working through problems.
tools.name: Claude
tools.start: Upload a long PDF and ask for the five most important points.

tools.desc: Google's AI chatbot. It works with Gmail, Google Docs and Google Maps, makes pictures and video, and can hold a live spoken conversation.
tools.name: Gemini
tools.start: Ask it to plan a day out near you using Google Maps.

tools.bestFor: People who use Windows and Office
tools.desc: Microsoft's AI helper. It is built into Windows, the Edge browser and Microsoft 365 apps such as Word, Excel and Outlook.
tools.name: Microsoft Copilot
tools.start: Open Copilot in Windows and ask it to sum up a web page you are reading.

tools.desc: A search engine that answers in plain language. It shows a numbered source for each fact, so you can check it.
tools.name: Perplexity
tools.start: Ask something you would normally search for. Then click the sources to check them.

tools.desc: Upload your own notes, PDFs or videos and ask questions about them. It can also turn them into a spoken summary that sounds like a podcast. It was called NotebookLM until July 2026.
tools.name: Gemini Notebook
tools.start: Upload a document you need to understand and make an audio summary of it.

tools.desc: Checks spelling, grammar and tone as you type in emails, documents and websites. It can also rewrite sentences for you.
tools.name: Grammarly
tools.start: Add it to your web browser, then write an email as usual.

tools.desc: AI inside the Notion notes app. It sums up notes, drafts pages and lists the action items from meeting notes.
tools.name: Notion AI
tools.start: Paste meeting notes into a page and ask for a list of action items.

tools.desc: Records meetings and calls, types out what people say as they talk, and writes a summary afterward.
tools.name: Otter.ai
tools.start: Record your next video call and read the summary afterward.

tools.desc: Makes striking, artistic pictures from a description. Designers and illustrators use it a lot.
tools.name: Midjourney
tools.start: Describe a scene, including a style and the lighting. Then try small changes.

tools.desc: A picture maker that is good at putting readable words into pictures, such as posters and logos.
tools.name: Ideogram
tools.start: Make a birthday card with the person's name written on it.

tools.desc: Adobe's picture and video maker. It was trained on content Adobe has permission to use, so it is designed to be safe for business use.
tools.name: Adobe Firefly
tools.start: Make a background for a product photo, then edit it in Photoshop or Adobe Express.

tools.desc: An easy design app. Its built-in AI writes text, makes pictures and resizes your designs.
tools.name: Canva
tools.start: Pick a template for a social media post and ask the AI to write the caption.

tools.desc: An AI video studio. It turns text or a photo into short clips, removes backgrounds and helps you edit.
tools.name: Runway
tools.start: Upload a photo and ask it to bring the scene to life.

tools.desc: Makes realistic short video clips from a description or a picture. You get a free allowance each day.
tools.name: Kling
tools.start: Describe a five-second scene, such as waves at sunset with birds flying past.

tools.desc: Makes whole songs, with singing and instruments, from a short description or your own lyrics.
tools.name: Suno
tools.start: Ask for a cheerful folk song about your pet.

tools.desc: Turns text into natural-sounding speech in many voices and languages. People use it for audiobooks and videos, and to make writing easier to listen to.
tools.name: ElevenLabs
tools.start: Paste in a paragraph and listen to it in three different voices.

tools.desc: A code editor with AI built in. Describe a change in plain English, and it edits the code across your project.
tools.name: Cursor
tools.start: Open a small project and ask it to explain what the code does.

tools.bestFor: Programmers using VS Code and GitHub
tools.desc: An AI coding helper inside popular code editors. It suggests code as you type and can take on whole tasks.
tools.name: GitHub Copilot
tools.start: Add it to VS Code, then write a comment that describes a function you need.

tools.desc: A coding agent. It reads your project, plans changes, writes and tests code, and explains what it did.
tools.name: Claude Code
tools.start: Ask it to add a small feature to a project, and read its plan before it starts.

tools.name: CoCounsel Legal
tools.desc: Thomson Reuters' AI assistant for lawyers. It draws on Westlaw and Practical Law content for research, and it can review documents and draft.
tools.start: Ask it to sum up a case you have already read, and compare its summary with the case.

tools.name: EverlawAI
tools.desc: AI features in the Everlaw e-discovery platform. It can sum up batches of documents, suggest coding and help draft from the evidence.
tools.start: Ask it to sum up a small set of documents, then check each summary against the documents.

tools.name: Harvey
tools.desc: An AI platform built for law firms and legal departments. It helps with research, drafting and reviewing large sets of documents.
tools.start: Try it on a closed matter or made-up documents during a trial, and check its answers against your own work.

tools.name: Lexis+ with Protégé
tools.desc: The LexisNexis legal research service with Protégé, its AI assistant. It answers research questions with links to cases and statutes, helps with drafting and can check citations with Shepard's. It was called Lexis+ AI until February 2026.
tools.start: Ask a research question you already know the answer to, then read every case it cites.

tools.name: Relativity aiR
tools.desc: AI for e-discovery. It uses language models to predict which documents are relevant to a lawsuit and explains why.
tools.start: Compare its relevance calls with a sample your team has already reviewed by hand.

tools.name: Spellbook
tools.desc: Contract drafting and review inside Microsoft Word. It suggests clauses, flags risky terms and proposes changes.
tools.start: Open a made-up contract in Word and ask it to list unusual or one-sided terms.

models.desc: A design for AI models, described in the 2017 research paper "Attention Is All You Need." Almost every modern language model is built on it.
models.name: The Transformer

models.desc: Read each sentence in both directions at once, which greatly improved how well computers understood language. Google soon used it to improve Google Search.
models.name: BERT

models.desc: Wrote paragraphs that sounded surprisingly human. At first, OpenAI held back the full version because of worries about misuse.
models.name: GPT-2

models.desc: Had 175 billion parameters. It was the first model that could write, translate, answer questions and write code from simple instructions.
models.name: GPT-3

models.desc: Predicted the 3D shapes of proteins, which had been a puzzle in biology for 50 years. Its creators shared the 2024 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
models.name: AlphaFold 2

models.desc: Showed that AI could draw pictures from a written description. It started the boom in AI pictures.
models.name: DALL·E

models.desc: Turned requests in plain English into working code. It ran the first version of GitHub Copilot.
models.name: Codex

models.desc: A free picture maker that anyone could download, run and change. A huge community of tools grew up around it.
models.name: Stable Diffusion

models.desc: Reached 100 million users in about two months and made AI chatbots part of everyday life.
models.name: ChatGPT launches

models.desc: Could read pictures as well as text. It scored well on hard professional exams, such as the bar exam for lawyers.
models.name: GPT-4

models.desc: Built with a strong focus on safety. It was one of the first models that could read very long documents in one go.
models.name: Claude and Claude 2

models.desc: A capable language model that anyone could download and build on. It gave researchers and small companies access to chatbot technology.
models.name: Llama 2

models.desc: Google's first model designed from the start to handle text, pictures, sound and video together.
models.name: Gemini 1.0

models.desc: Introduced three sizes, called Haiku, Sonnet and Opus. Claude 3.5 Sonnet became a favorite for coding and writing.
models.name: Claude 3 and 3.5

models.desc: Could hold natural voice conversations in real time and see through your camera. The "o" stands for "omni," which means "all."
models.name: GPT-4o

models.desc: The first widely used thinking model. It works step by step before it answers, which makes it much better at math and logic.
models.name: o1

models.desc: Free-to-download models that came close to the best paid models of their time.
models.name: Llama 3

models.desc: Made realistic video clips from a written description. It was a big step for AI video.
models.name: Sora

models.desc: A free thinking model from a Chinese company. Anyone could download it, and it matched top paid models for a small part of the cost.
models.name: DeepSeek-R1

models.desc: Made video with matching sound, speech and music, all from one description.
models.name: Veo 3

models.desc: Claude Opus 4 and Sonnet 4 could work on coding and agent tasks for hours at a time.
models.name: Claude 4

models.desc: Google's first models with thinking built in. They could read about a million tokens of text at once.
models.name: Gemini 2.5

models.desc: Combined fast answers and deeper thinking in one system that decides how long to think.
models.name: GPT-5

models.desc: Anthropic's current models. They include Haiku 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Opus 5.5, plus Claude Fable 5.2, its most capable public model, released in November 2026. Claude Mythos 5.2 is the same model without some of Fable's safety limits for cybersecurity and biology, and only approved organizations can use it.
models.name: Claude 5 family

models.desc: OpenAI's current models. In November 2026 it released GPT-6.2 Astra, its most capable model for hard projects, and GPT-6.2 Sol, a cheaper model for everyday work. ChatGPT's free plan uses GPT-6 Luna.
models.name: GPT-6 family

models.desc: Google's current models, introduced in October 2026. Gemini 4 Argon is the most capable. Carbon, Neon and Hydrogen handle everyday tasks in Gemini and other Google products. Neon was added in November 2026 as a faster, cheaper middle option.
models.name: Gemini 4 family
